# Opus 5.5 code-rendered videos: research notes

> Research date: October 2026. Goal: study the wave of "Opus 5.5 writes code that makes a video" works and pull out methods this studio can use directly (the `window.draw(t)` frame-by-frame pipeline in `tools/code_anim/render.py`, Three.js, Blender), then propose new skills.
>

Downloaded the README and `data/videos.json`. **The current count is not the ~282 mentioned in the task**: the README says "703 prompts in `prompts/` and `data/videos.json`, 418 of them with a live remake on Skillry", last updated 2026-10-12. Categories in the json: motion 369 / 3d 117 / explainer 116 / interactive 101. Most common tech tags: canvas 267, svg 183, threejs 131, shader 92, gsap 86, css 57, audio 39.

## 0. One-page summary (TL;DR)

1. **These videos are not generated by an "AI video model"**: Opus writes a **program that draws frames** (HTML/Canvas/SVG/Three.js/Remotion/Blender Python), headless Chrome (Playwright/Puppeteer) or Blender renders it frame by frame, and ffmpeg muxes the MP4. OrcaRouter puts it this way: "Il écrit du code qui peint des pixels. Le résultat est un programme, pas un fichier vidéo." ("It writes code that paints pixels. The result is a program, not a video file.") Our `render.py` already follows the same route.
2. **The most-liked works all follow one iron rule**: **"every frame is a pure function of time"**, i.e. each frame depends only on the time t. No CSS transitions, no timers, no unseeded random numbers. Frames can be rendered in any order, and rendering the same frame twice gives identical pixels (yankis0x, parkerrex, 0xKarmi and everestchris6 all list this as rule number one).
3. **High-quality prompts have an almost fixed structure**: `<inputs>` (ask the user for assets first) → `<direction>` (style: one typeface, a palette down to exact hex values, **a list of banned effects**) → `<structure>` (a 120 BPM beat grid, one event per beat) → `<build>` (technical constraints + render method) → `<gotchas>/<quality_bar>` (measurable acceptance criteria) → `<start>` (storyboard before code).
4. **The key to "not looking like AI" is restraint**: one typeface (Geist/Inter), three to five colors, one accent color, "one idea per shot"; explicitly ban particle bursts, glows, lens flares, camera shake, RGB split and bouncy easing; use critically damped springs with no overshoot.
5. **Quality control is a process**: first a contact sheet (16–20 frames tiled into one image), then a 5-second sample, and only then the full render; review is handed to "a fresh critic that has not seen the build"; no more than about 1 second of frozen screen per 30 seconds, text contrast ≥ 4.5:1, loudness -14 LUFS.
6. **Topics most relevant to our channel**: floor plan → 3D house (aayush4soni); a house that builds itself in five stages with X-ray, section cut and dusk modes (MrKindey); a pencil sketch growing into a house (cryptowluha); 45° sunlight in a cathedral (AGIOyaZ, vertical 1080×1920); exploded views of a heart, a V8 and a turbofan (aichrislee, 0xSpikez); a continuous zoom from a desk down to an atom (Acoramaa); 15 Chinese-language 10-second templates (NFT_Chen).
7. **There are few vertical works**: only 10 entries in the json mention "9:16" and 20 mention "vertical"; most are 16:9 or 1:1 (1440×1440). So adapting these methods to Chinese-language vertical video is a differentiator in itself.

## 1. How these videos are actually made

### 1.1 Tech stack (by frequency and role)

| Layer | Common choices | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 2D visuals | Canvas 2D (most common), SVG, CSS | json tags canvas 267 / svg 183 / css 57 |
| Animation orchestration | GSAP timelines, Remotion (React → video), HyperFrames (HTML → video) | in the json prompt text "remotion" appears 113 times and "hyperframes" 25 times; Skillry pages list GSAP / Remotion / HyperFrames |
| 3D | Three.js (WebGL), Three.js + TSL/WebGPU, raw WebGPU/WGSL, GLSL shaders | threejs 131 / shader 92; e.g. thebuggeddev's "procedural Three.js WebGPU and TSL shaders" |
| Blender | Blender Python scripts build the scene, EEVEE/Cycles render it | "blender" appears 17 times in prompts; oab10don uses Cycles; wikiwayne builds the same clay scene "First in Blender, then in Three.js" |
| Math explainers | Manim (3Blue1Brown style) | eleanorina "FrankenManim … 3b1b-style"; athemeroy lists LinearUncle's "Manim + edge-tts derivatives lesson" |
| Narration TTS | ElevenLabs, OpenAI TTS, Gemini TTS, Microsoft TTS (edge-tts), CosyVoice, open-source TTS | l3d1c (ElevenLabs), HenriToivar (OpenAI TTS), deedydas (gemini 3.8 tts), HenrygSing ("generate the voice locally with Microsoft's TTS. Free." — translated from Chinese) |
| Music and SFX | Python/numpy synthesis (sine waves + noise), Web Audio synthesis, royalty-free Mixkit tracks, Suno | daniel-haida: "the soundtrack is code too, synthesized in python from sine waves and noise"; oab10don: "kick, snare, bass and synth synthesized in numpy code" (translated from Japanese) |
| Capture and export | Playwright / Puppeteer / Node drive headless Chrome to screenshot each frame, ffmpeg encodes; Remotion has its own renderer | yankis0x: "Playwright renders -> ffmpeg blends"; OrcaRouter: "A Node script drives headless Chrome and captures each frame… ~3,760 frames… 156.6 seconds at 24 fps" |
| Post | ffmpeg `tmix` sub-frame motion blur, loudnorm to -14 LUFS; a few people grade in DaVinci | twoclipping, yankis0x; a Skillry page mentions DaVinci Resolve |

**"Screen recordings of interactive web pages" are the second major source**: many 3D hits (heart, V8, lens, rocket engine, house) are actually **interactive single-file HTML pages** (drag to rotate, an Explode button) that the author **screen-recorded** and posted. StefanoStraus says: "This is a screen recording, the real thing runs live in your browser". [My suggestion] We don't screen-record; instead we rewrite the "interaction" as a **scripted timeline** (camera path and explode progress are both functions of t), so we can render a 60 fps vertical video frame by frame with no dropped frames.

### 1.2 Reusable "render pipeline" quotes

- **yankis0x** (<https://x.com/yankis0x/status/2103502194578174321>):
  > "The trick is NOT the prompt. It is one rule: every frame is a pure function of time. song -> numpy beat grid -> Opus 5.5 writes one HTML file -> Playwright renders -> ffmpeg blends … one HTML file, 1440x1440, every style computed inside seek(t). no CSS transitions, no timers … springs as closed-form math, so any frame renders in any order … Playwright shoots 4 subframes per frame, ffmpeg tmix blends them into 60fps motion blur … render one frame per beat first, fix what is off the grid, then the full render"
- **0xKarmi** (<https://x.com/0xKarmi/status/2108495927988129839>):
  > "STAGE - one fixed 1000x1080 canvas, fonts baked in > RENDER - a windowless engine calls draw(f) once per frame number > ENCODE - ffmpeg writes H.264 … > CHECK - three passes after every build … The seam check puts frame 0 against frame 720. One changed pixel means some motion isn't periodic."

  This is the same thing as our `window.draw(t)` convention.
- **okazaky** (vertical MV, <https://x.com/okazaky/status/2107826563786084783>):
  > "Create a 50-second vertical music video using programmatic rendering (Three.js) … 3. Transcribe vocals with mlx_whisper … '1 lyric line = 1 scene'. 4. Write storyboard: define 'What to show in 3D', 'Camera', 'Main word' for each lyric line. 5. Have 4 parallel Opus sub-agents write scene programs. 6. Export 16-frame contact sheet for visual verification. 7. Render headless Chrome at 1080x1920, 60fps. 8. Normalize volume to -14 LUFS. Style: Engraving-like lines, colors limited to Black, Bone, Orange."
- **twoclipping** (Hooklab brief, <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/twoclipping-000267>), the `<build>` section:
  > "Every style is computed from time inside window.seek(t): no CSS animations, no timers, no state between frames. … Real video: extract clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg and swap img sources per frame. seek awaits the image decodes. … Render with Playwright: 3 subframes per frame at t minus, at, and plus 1/240s, then blend with ffmpeg tmix for real motion blur at 60fps. … Place each sound effect so its measured peak, not its file start, lands on the event. … Loudnorm to -14 LUFS. … Probe 20 or more frames before the full render."

  `<gotchas>`: "Never set opacity or filter on a preserve-3d element, because it flattens and both faces show. Fade its wrapper instead."
- **l3d1c** (9:16 ad, <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/l3d1c-632524>):
  > "It rendered about 20 stills and tiled them into one contact sheet, so I could check a whole cut at a glance before rendering any video. Captions are measured in the real font and shrink to fit the 9:16 safe zone, so nothing hides under TikTok's buttons. Every cut lands on a 120 BPM grid … the 30s, 15s and 6s cuts in 16:9 and 9:16 are each a different list of scenes."

### 1.3 Duration and aspect ratio

- **Duration**: athemeroy analyzed 1,401 X video files; the **median preview duration is 39.2 seconds** (interquartile range 21.9–77.1 s). Among 168 manually reviewed cases, **educational explainers have a median of 102.3 seconds**, while the other paths range 24.8–51.8 s (<https://github.com/athemeroy/awesome-opus-5-5-videos/blob/main/docs/snapshot-analysis.md>). The first 40 entries on the Skillry list page run 0:10–1:46, mostly 15–60 seconds. Prompts most often say "15s / 20.00s / 30s / 60s".
- **Aspect ratio**: in the prompt text "1920x1080" appears 14 times, "16:9" 18 times, "9:16" 10 times; square 1080×1080 / 1440×1440 is a frequent X-native choice (techhalla: "1080×1080 (square, X-native)"). Only a handful explicitly specify 1080×1920 vertical, such as AGIOyaZ, okazaky and GabZoFar (two versions).
- **Frame rate**: "60fps" appears 55 times, "30fps" 9 times.

### 1.4 How iteration really works (the truth about "one-shot")

- OrcaRouter points out that the supposedly one-shot PDoom MV was actually generated in **two rounds**: only after the first round did the model write its own `STORYBOARD.md` and animation guide, and the second round was revised against them. Also: "Determinism isn't automatic. The prompt didn't enforce it. The repos handled it."
- The 5 briefs athemeroy published range from **172 to 17,664 characters**. "One prompt" only says how many instructions the human sent; it doesn't mean there were no assets, no preinstalled skills and no revisions (last section of `docs/prompt-playbook.zh-CN.md`).
- Common multi-agent splits: Voxyz_ai's black-hole lab runs 3 agents per round: "Two reviewers each picked 9 to 10 issues and ranked them P0, P1, P2. The third one fixed them." (<https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/voxyz-ai-345550>); stokebuilder uses "extra-high effort to find the timings → medium effort to build → one extra-high effort review, No blanket redo loops".

## 2. The prompt patterns that work best

### 2.1 Skeleton: an XML-sectioned brief (the shared structure of viral templates)

The widely reshared twoclipping template family (at least 10 near-verbatim copies in the json, e.g. morse, demonugc, nezbuilds, hiCallMeChai…) and everestchris6's master brief share almost the same structure:

| Section | What it contains | Example quote |
|---|---|---|
| `<inputs>` | Make the model **ask you** for assets first, with defaults if any are missing | "Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states … and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM … If I skip any, use the defaults" |
| `<direction>` | Style, typeface, palette, **banned list** | "High-end minimal. One idea per shot, lots of empty space, one accent color, one clean sans (Geist or Inter) with tight tracking. … Banned: shockwave rings, particle bursts, RGB split, camera shake, lens flares, neon glows, grid floors, flashing backgrounds, bouncy easing." |
| `<structure>` | Beat grid and bar-by-bar storyboard | "10 bars at 120 BPM, 2 seconds each. Bar 1: the hook lands word by word on the beats." |
| `<build>` | Technical constraints and render method | see 1.2 |
| `<gotchas>` / `<quality_bar>` | Measurable acceptance criteria | see 2.4 |
| `<start>` | Storyboard first, then code | "Ask me for the inputs, then show me a storyboard with every timing on the beat grid before you write any code." |

One line from flxrnc is key (<https://x.com/flxrnc/status/2108242454105251921>):
> "Use hex codes, seconds, damping ratios and pixel sizes instead of adjectives."

### 2.2 Details prompts usually spell out

1. **An exact palette (hex) with a job for each color**: heyiamnick writes "paper cream #EDE6D5, blueprint blue #1B3ED2, hologram cyan #45F0DD … Each stage's accent is the next stage's colour"; techhalla writes "PALETTE (strict) … No other hues".
2. **Typeface, weight and tracking**: "Geist only. Weight 900 for big words, 600 to 800 for small labels (24 to 28 px, tracked 0.14 to 0.3 em)" (heyiamnick).
3. **Easing written as a formula**: "a critically damped spring, 1 - (1 + w t) e^(-w t) with w between 12 and 40, so nothing ever passes its target" (heyiamnick); "Shape damping 0.72, settle time 0.35s. Camera damping 1.0, settle time 0.6s" (flxrnc); "Every morph glides for 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1)" (rossaxbt / twoclipping-762046).
4. **Camera language locked down**: "Camera: locked and front-on for the whole film, like a drafting table. Objects turn; the camera never moves." (heyiamnick); for 3D, "keep the camera between about 35 and 55 degrees. never look straight down on a large surface" (everestchris6).
5. **A to-the-second timeline**: AGIOyaZ's "0–3 s … 3–11 s … 11–14 s: Total darkness and silence. 14–19 s …".
6. **Single file, zero external resources**: "Create a single self-contained HTML file … No external assets, libraries, or network requests." (zacxbt / majidmanzarpour); "No images. Do not ask me any questions. Just build it." (the aichrislee series).
7. **Real data and sources**: "Include real numbers … and be honest about uncertainty" (AstroTheWizard); "facts file: [path]. this is the only source for any number, name or claim that appears on screen" (everestchris6); "No invented results: no %, multipliers, customer names or figures." (ik_builds).
8. **Safe margins**: "nothing at rest within 150 px of the sides or 90 px of the top and bottom" (heyiamnick); "Keep text clear of the TikTok/Instagram interface. Let viewers follow: each feature stays on screen for at least 2.5 seconds" (Bilimfili1).
9. **Autonomous runs**: "I'm stepping away from my computer, so work autonomously until it's done." (AstroTheWizard)

### 2.3 Two cases where short prompts still shine

- **The object itself is very information-dense** (heart, watch, V8, lens): aichrislee's template is only about 800 characters, but it names the "invisible internal parts" one by one and adds a fixed interaction trio (orbit/zoom, Explode + labels, hover shows a one-line explanation).
- **A preinstalled skill or framework already exists**: ik_builds' 15-second template, emollick's recursive video (159 characters), parkerrex's "explain a token bucket rate limiter, canvas only, no libraries, every frame a pure function of time so my renderer can screenshot it." (133 characters, <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/parkerrex-701462>). **Short prompts work because the renderer conventions were agreed in advance**, which is exactly the value of a skill.

### 2.4 Measurable acceptance criteria (everestchris6, the most complete)

<https://x.com/everestchris6/status/2104965415164399895>
> "no more than about 1 second of frozen screen per 30 seconds, and no still stretch longer than about half a second / frame one is a finished composition / all text meets at least 4.5:1 contrast, and nothing collides with or flies through other text / … loudness is steady and comfortable for web, with no clipping, and effects never louder than the music / a first-time viewer understands it with the sound off / … a video with no bugs is not the same as a good video"

The critic loop:
> "the builder never judges its own work … send the render, the brief and the references to a fresh critic that has seen none of the building … the critic makes a contact sheet every 0.2 seconds plus dense frames around every transition … returns a ranked list of problems with timestamps, ending with ship or one more pass … keep a ledger of every round"

### 2.5 Common mistakes (as mentioned in the sources)

| Mistake | Source |
|---|---|
| Frames depend on state, timers or unseeded random numbers, causing flicker when rendered in parallel | OrcaRouter: "Frames render in parallel and out of order, so stored state or uninitialized randomness will cause flicker." |
| The program looks fine, then crashes minutes into the render | OrcaRouter: "Failures are silent." |
| Setting opacity/filter directly on a preserve-3d element | twoclipping gotchas |
| The first frame is text halfway through flying in | everestchris6: "frame one is a finished picture, never a word halfway through flying in" |
| Small cards floating in a sea of empty space, or every scene is "heading + three cards" | everestchris6: "no small cards floating in empty space … never repeat the same layout, like a heading over three cards" |
| Putting 3D text inside the scene | everestchris6: "labels are html positioned from the 3d scene every frame, never text inside the 3d" |
| Aligning SFX by file start instead of by peak | twoclipping: "Place each sound effect so its measured peak, not its file start, lands on the event" |
| Animation jargon ("easing", "stagger") or UI chrome (timecode, fps) showing on screen | ik_builds |
| Invented numbers or customers | ik_builds, everestchris6 |
| The first version is weak and needs feedback | a Skillry page notes an author whose first version was weak and only improved after pushing back; apoorvjain25 "took several prompts" |
| No captions by default, so it's incomprehensible with the sound off | AstroTheWizard: "Burned-in captions, since most people watch on X with the sound off" |

## 3. The 15 examples most relevant to this studio

> Selection criteria: architecture/interiors, 3D science teardowns, data/process explainers, vertical format, Chinese language. "Skillry" means a detail page (only entries with a remake have one); otherwise the X post is given.

### A. Architecture / interiors (floor plan → CAD → 3D → sunlight)

**1. Floor-plan PDF → walkable 3D house**: @aayush4soni (3D, Three.js)
Skillry: <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/aayush4soni-644283> · X: <https://x.com/aayush4soni/status/2104181266459644283>
Key quote (author's notes, not the prompt itself):
> "I gave it the 5-page floor-plan PDF and one reference image for the front of the house. • It read the drawings and rebuilt every floor: walls, doors, windows and stairs. • Where a printed size didn't match the drawn wall, it flagged it (15 places) instead of quietly guessing. • It furnished every room itself: 500+ pieces of furniture, decor and lighting. • Everything runs in a web browser with three.js. … in daylight or evening light, and the lamps actually light the rooms. • … ~37k lines of JavaScript, 185 unit tests, 56 browser tests, and deterministic video capture (render the same frame twice, get identical pixels)."

Why it works: a real need ("walk through the house before building it"), eye-level camera, two lighting setups (day and dusk). When dimensions disagree it **flags them instead of guessing**, which is worth writing into our floor-plan skill. It took about two days and several sub-agents, showing that a full interior walkthrough is heavy work; a short video only needs 3–4 shots from it.

**2. A house that builds itself in five stages (X-ray, explode, section cut, dusk)**: @MrKindey (Three.js on WebGPU, single HTML)
X: <https://x.com/MrKindey/status/2107817784432267498>
> "an interactive 3D house that builds itself in five stages: Foundation → Skeleton → Systems → Envelope → Finished. Every part has its own window on the timeline, so you can scrub through the construction like a video. … X-ray mode … shows the water, power, sewage and airflow routes … Explode … Cut, a section plane that slices through the building … Dusk, a lighting switch … Callouts and preset cameras for each stage"

The matching short prompt (@techartist_, <https://x.com/techartist_/status/2105350783416021472>):
> "Create an interactive 3D house animation showing the construction process from Foundation through Skeleton, Systems and Envelope to Finished. Include an X-ray view that reveals the plumbing, power and air inside. Use Three.js and WebGPU."

Why it works: **"every part has its own window on the timeline" is exactly the `draw(t)` idea** and can be lifted directly: each component gets a `[t0,t1]` growth window. The three "reveal" moves (X-ray, section plane, dusk switch) make good section beats.

**3. A pencil sketch growing into a house (four stages)**: @cryptowluha (Three.js + TSL)
X: <https://x.com/cryptowluha/status/2108253385829060792>
> "Create a 3D animation showing a house growing out of a pencil sketch, line by line. The animation should progress through four stages: first lines, massing, detail, and finished home. Use Three.js and TSL for implementation."

Why it works: "line drawing → massing → detail → finished" is the generic version of the "floor plan → CAD → 3D" narrative, and suits a 15–20 second vertical opener.

**4. One model producing 14 drawings + 5 calculations + 3D + CAD export**: @AJtheMongol
Skillry: <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/ajthemongol-318512>
> "Designed a house as a code with Opus 5.5 / One model -> 14 drawings, 5 engineering calculations, a 3D viewer and a CAD export / Concept only, not stamped"

Why it works: **"one data model drives both the drawings and the 3D"**. [My suggestion] The floor-plan skill should first write a `plan.json` (walls, doors, windows, rooms, dimensions) and generate both the 2D CAD linework and the 3D extrusion from it, so plan and 3D dimensions always agree. It is also labelled "Concept only, not stamped"; our renovation/floor-plan explainers should likewise say "for illustration only".

**5. 45° sunlight in a cathedral, vertical 1080×1920**: @AGIOyaZ (Three.js, 37 seconds, 30 fps)
X: <https://x.com/AGIOyaZ/status/2103167623303397647>
Excerpt (the original uses full-width lenticular brackets around section names, shown here as square brackets):
> "Create a 37-second vertical short film (1080×1920, 30 fps) in three.js, titled "White Space". … - Strong sunlight enters from outside at 45°, casting the window's image onto the stone floor. … [Timeline] 0–3 s: Colorless white light fills the cathedral. 3–11 s: Gray cubes engraved with words fly in faster and faster, sealing the window. The room darkens. 11–14 s: Total darkness and silence. 14–19 s: Only the "BUSY" block falls away … One golden beam enters. … [Music and sound (original, synthesized)] - 0–11 s: A ticking clock that accelerates; a dull thud each time a block lands … 11–14 s: Silence - 14.8 s: A single crystalline bell as the first beam enters"

Why it works: a rare **vertical-native prompt with Chinese-style bracketed section headers**. The light itself is the protagonist, and the to-the-second timeline **deliberately leaves 3 seconds of total darkness and silence**. It shows how a "sunlight/daylighting" topic can carry emotion, and is a direct reference for floor-plan sunlight topics like "south-facing windows and the winter-solstice sun angle".

### B. 3D science teardowns (heart, engines)

**6. Human heart (interactive 3D template, single HTML)**: @aichrislee (Three.js + Canvas + Web Audio, 0:16)
Skillry: <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/aichrislee-378670>
Full text:
> "Build me a human heart in interactive 3D, in one HTML file with Three.js.
> Make it look real: the deep red muscle with the red arteries and blue veins on top, and inside it the parts you never get to see. The four chambers, the four valves, the aorta and the pulmonary artery, the veins bringing blood back, and the wiring that sets the beat. The heart beats about once a second, the valves open and close in time, and the blood flows through it, blue going in and red going out. I can drag to orbit around it and scroll to zoom.
> Add an Explode button. When I press it, every part slides apart with its name on a label. Press it again and it all snaps back together. When I hover a part, it lights up and shows one line on what it does.
> No images. Do not ask me any questions. Just build it."

Why it works: it is a **template with a swappable subject**. The same author has used it for a V8 (<https://x.com/aichrislee/status/2107260223907922082>), a mechanical watch (<https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/aichrislee-476025>), a camera lens (<https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/aichrislee-408244>), the Saturn V and a jet engine. The structure is a fixed three parts: (1) key points on exterior materials, (2) name the "parts you never get to see" one by one, (3) the motion rules (heartbeat about once a second, valves in sync) + explode + labels + one-line explanation.

**7. V8 engine**: @aichrislee
X: <https://x.com/aichrislee/status/2107260223907922082>
> "… the engine block with its two banks of cylinders in a V, the pistons and connecting rods, the crankshaft, the camshafts and valves on top, the intake manifold and the exhaust headers glowing hot. The pistons pump up and down, the crankshaft turns, and the spark plugs flash when each cylinder fires. …"

Why it works: the motion is causal (spark plug fires → piston → crankshaft), and mechanical motion is naturally a periodic function of t, which makes it ideal for deterministic rendering.

**8. Turbofan engine with labelled stages**: @0xSpikez (0:23)
Skillry: <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/0xspikez-483865>
> "an interactive 3D turbofan you can take apart in the browser, built with Three.js. suck, squeeze, bang, blow, every stage labelled: > the fan pulls in a huge mass of air. most of it bypasses the core and makes most of the thrust > compressor stages squeeze the air about 40 times, heating it > fuel burns hotter than the turbine metal's melting point > the blades survive on cooling air and heat-resistant coatings > two shafts, one inside the other, spinning at different speeds then it explodes into every stage."

Why it works: **each stage comes with one counter-intuitive fact** ("the fuel burns hotter than the turbine metal's melting point"). That is exactly our explainer "hook line", and it can serve directly as the skeleton for a 9-line script.

### C. Zooms, processes, data explainers

**9. From a desk all the way down to one silicon atom (one continuous shot + scale ruler)**: @Acoramaa (Three.js)
Skillry: <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/acoramaa-053577>
> "start at my desk and don't stop zooming until we hit a single atom inside the CPU. … Into the PC case. The cooler lifts off. The CPU under it. The metal lid comes off. Then the silicon die, one core, the copper wiring stacked on top, rows of logic cells, the fins and gates of the transistors… …all the way down to one silicon atom, bonded to its four neighbours. One continuous shot, no cuts. The ruler on the right tracks the scale the whole time: from about a metre down to about 2 nanometres."

Similar: VictorTaelin "starts in a room, zooms into a MacBook, then into an Apple M4 chip, followed by atoms, and finally quarks" (<https://x.com/VictorTaelin/status/2103299766473875778>).
Why it works: the **always-visible scale ruler on the side** gives viewers a "scale anchor", and with "no cuts" the completion rate is high. Good for topics like "from a grain of rice to a city" or "from the neighborhood to the floor plan to the layers inside one wall".

**10. Earthquake: plates → seismic waves → a shaking city**: @egeberkina (60 seconds)
X: <https://x.com/egeberkina/status/2105029713445949521>
> "Make it feel like we are watching someone explore a beautiful real-time simulation, not a slideshow or traditional educational video. … Visualize P-waves and S-waves traveling differently through the Earth … Show buildings reacting differently depending on distance from the epicenter. … The pacing should constantly evolve and reveal something new every few seconds … Make it feel like an Apple-quality interactive science visualization turned into a cinematic motion-design video."

Why it works: the framing "like watching a real simulation being explored, not a slideshow" can be used directly to fight the "PowerPoint feel". The structure is "build-up → release → spread → aftershocks → pull back for the big picture".

**11. A photon escaping the Sun's core (master brief for a high-quality explainer)**: @AstroTheWizard (60 seconds, 1920×1080)
Skillry: <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/astrothewizard-618782>
Excerpt:
> "It should feel like a professional motion-design studio made it, not "AI video". … what makes them great is that they're code-rendered: crisp, precise, with a coherent design system and one strong formal idea per scene. … Where you can, simulate the real thing: the random walk should be an actual random walk, not a drawing of one. Include real numbers … and be honest about uncertainty in the estimates. … Burned-in captions … An original music score … Sound design synced exactly to the on-screen action (every bounce, pop, whoosh and ding) - A professional mix: music ducks under the voice, mastered to streaming loudness … Build verification loops: render stills of every scene and review them critically … measure the audio mix numerically … Don't hand me a first draft."

Why it works: "**actually simulate it, don't draw something that looks like a simulation**" is the most valuable rule for explainers. Compound interest, probability and random walks should all be computed, not hand-placed curves. Our kp series already does this.

**12. 15 Chinese-language 10-second templates (shadow puppetry / isometric process / scale comparison / 3B1B / Kurzgesagt / exploded view…)**: @NFT_Chen
X: <https://x.com/NFT_Chen/status/2107653056771068069>
Excerpt (translated from Chinese; the brackets mark the swappable subject):
> "Use three.js to make a 12-second exploded view taking apart [a phone]. The shell, mid-frame and chips burst apart in layers, the camera orbits and pushes in, and parts get dashed leader-line labels. Swap in any structure."
> "Make a 10-second scale comparison placing [Earth, Jupiter and the Sun] side by side at their real radii. The camera pulls back smoothly, the first object shrinks, and it lands the point: 'About 1.3 million Earths fit inside the Sun.' Numbers clearly labelled."
> "Make a 10-second 3Blue1Brown-style math visualization about [the area of a circle]. Dark background; the circle is cut into 8, 16, 32 sectors that really slide and reassemble into a rectangle. The formula appears term by term and holds on πr²."
> "Make a 12-second isometric 2.5D process animation about [how parcels get sorted]. … Each step gets a numbered label, and at the end the two lines merge into one. Clean and easy to follow."
> "Make a 10-second beat-synced typography piece, 120 BPM, about [the Feynman technique]. One word per beat, orange text cutting in on black. The four steps slam in one after another, and the final hit: if you can't explain it clearly, you don't really understand it."

Why it works: the format **"style name + duration + [swappable subject] + 2–3 concrete actions + a punchline"** is ideal for building a topic library, and covers most of our content directions. Note they are all only 10–12 seconds: they are "clip-level" templates that can serve as one shot inside a kp video.

**13. A Chinese-language workflow: script + director's notes → STORYBOARD.md → Remotion scene by scene → Microsoft TTS**: @HenrygSing

It writes STORYBOARD.md first, spelling out the timing, visuals, text and transition for every scene. Then it builds one scene at a time in Remotion. And one more thing: it generates the voice locally with Microsoft's TTS. Free."

### D. Style and pipeline exemplars

**14. One pencil line "promoted" three times: paper → blueprint → hologram**: @heyiamnick (Canvas, 0:30)
Skillry: <https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/heyiamnick-119558>
> "Concept, in one line: one pencil line gets promoted three times (graphite on paper, wire on a blueprint, light on black) and never leaves the screen. Every shot is made out of the previous one … No cuts, no fades. … BLUEPRINT: flat blue with the same grid in white. Clean white lines 3 to 4 px, hidden edges dashed and thinner, fills are fine clean hatching. … PAPER: … Lines are pencil: resampled and pushed off true by slow sine waves whose phase changes 8 times a second, stroked twice (full width at 90%, half width at 40% with more wobble) …"

Why it works: it is a **ready-made art spec for "hand-drawn floor plan → CAD blueprint → 3D hologram"**. The pencil line recipe ("sine-wave wobble whose phase changes 8 times a second + double stroke") can go straight into Canvas code, and the blueprint's "hidden edges dashed and thinner" is standard CAD drafting convention.

It is the only vertical case that spells out **1080×1920, 60 fps, headless Chrome, a 16-frame contact sheet and 4 parallel sub-agents** all together, and can serve directly as the process template for our "lyrics/quote vertical" videos.

## 4. Visual lessons for looking premium and "not AI"

1. **Typography**: one sans-serif for the whole piece (Geist/Inter), with weight creating the hierarchy (900 for big words, 600–800 for small labels, small labels with wide tracking of 0.14–0.3em). When a literary feel is needed, use the trio "high-contrast serif + heavy grotesque + small monospace marks" (Gdgtify's "BUILD THE FLOOR": "a high-contrast serif for the speech, a heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, and a restrained monospace for small timing marks"). [My suggestion] Chinese equivalents: Source Han Sans Heavy for big words, Source Han Serif for literary lines, a monospace font for numbers and dimension labels.
2. **Palette**: 3–5 colors, **one accent color**, every color with a job (background, ink, accent). athemeroy's color study found motion/UI works split into two camps, **dark neutral (198) and light neutral (152)**; in ads the median share of "colorful pixels" is only **17.6%**, versus 45.5% for MVs. Conclusion: **explainer and ad visuals are mostly neutral, with color used only as an accent**.
3. **A banned list is more useful than a recommended list**: particle bursts, shockwave rings, glows, lens flares, camera shake, RGB split, grid floors, flashing backgrounds, bouncy easing, crossfades, generic gradients, "anything that looks like a template".
4. **Motion**: critically damped springs, no overshoot; "things land slowly enough to read, leave fast"; one primary motion with a few secondary ones, "the frame never stops and starts all at once" (everestchris6 motion principles 3–4).
5. **Transitions**: the foreground object is the transition (a title or object rushes at the camera while the next scene is already waiting underneath); one object carries through several shots; hard cuts only when size, direction and subject all match; continuous morphing with "no cuts, no fades" is the hallmark of viral pieces.
6. **Pacing**: 12–15 compositions per 30 seconds, each 1.4–3.5 seconds; "a new idea every 1.5–2 s" (ik_builds); no still shot longer than about 0.5 seconds. Explainers can slow down, but each piece of information should stay on screen at least 2.5 seconds (Bilimfili1).
7. **3D lighting and materials**: "light it like a product shoot, with a soft key light from one side and a rim light behind … style buildings like a premium architectural model with real materials and a base … no floating parts, no gaps where parts meet, no flat black glass, no repeating textures" (everestchris6). For floor-plan 3D this is a **directly usable art standard**: the architectural model gets a base and solid materials such as white massing, wood-grain floors and frosted glass.
8. **Labels**: an HTML/2D overlay projected from 3D coordinates every frame, never text inside the 3D scene; part labels use dashed leader lines (NFT_Chen's exploded-view template).
9. **Sound design**: SFX only on "real on-screen actions" (a soft whoosh per scene change, a pop per click/landing); SFX aligned to events by **peak**; music ducks under the voice; overall -14 LUFS, -2 dBTP (ik_builds: "Master -14 LUFS, -2 dBTP, re-measured after AAC encode"). Code-synthesized music (numpy/Web Audio) can give "every action its own sound", e.g. iniyanai's mechanical-keyboard explainer: "used real switch recordings as the beats … timed every cut to the beat" (<https://skillry.dev/ai-videos/opus-5-5/iniyanai-856596>). A deliberate **silent stretch** (AGIOyaZ's 11–14 s) also hits hard.
10. **The first frame must be complete**, it must make sense with the sound off (captions burned into the picture), and there must be a hook within the first second (jhylee95: "hook in the first second").

## 5. Recommendations for our existing pipelines

### 5.1 Pattern → pipeline mapping

| Pattern in the collections | Existing pipeline | How to connect it ([My suggestion]) |
|---|---|---|
| `seek(t)`/`draw(f)` pure-function frames | `window.draw(t)` + `window.ready` in `render.py` | Already aligned. Add a hard rule: no state driven by `Date.now()`, `performance.now()` or `requestAnimationFrame`, and no `Math.random()` (use a seeded PRNG); add a self-check that "renders the same frame twice and compares hashes" |
| Sub-frame motion blur (3–4 sub-frames + ffmpeg tmix) | render.py currently captures once per frame | Add a `--motion-blur 3` option: capture at t-1/240, t and t+1/240, then blend with tmix. Enable only for fast-motion segments (3× screenshot cost) |
| Contact-sheet review | `--stills` outputs single screenshots | Add `--sheet 16`: sample 16 evenly spaced frames into a 4×4 grid, with dense sampling around each transition, so Claude can review the images itself |
| 120 BPM beat grid | Timeline currently laid out by TTS sentence durations | Keep explainers "sentence-driven"; make quote/beat-sync pieces "beat-driven": measure the BGM beats with numpy and snap cuts to the nearest beat |
| SFX aligned by peak + -14 LUFS | `mix()` uses loudnorm I=-16 | Douyin is fine at -16 to -14; add an SFX track (pop/whoosh at event times, aligned by peak), and duck the music under narration |
| Screen-recorded interactive 3D (Explode button, orbit) | `three_template.html` | Rewrite "interaction" as a timeline: `explode = smooth(t, t0, t1)`, the camera follows a spline `cam(t)`, hover highlighting becomes timed round-robin highlighting, and labels use a 2D canvas overlay positioned by 3D projection |
| 9:16 safe zone | Vertical 1080×1920 | Draw optional safe-zone guides in the template (on while debugging). Rule of thumb: keep key text out of roughly the top 150px, the bottom 400px (title, caption, buttons) and the right 160px (like bar). **These numbers are my own estimates and need calibrating against real Douyin screenshots** |
| Blender scripts building scenes | video-lineart (EEVEE + Freestyle) | Exploded views, white architectural massing and sunlight studies can all use the same "per-part time window" in Blender; real sunlight via the Blender Sun's azimuth/elevation interpolated over t looks better than Three.js shadows, at the cost of slow renders and machine heat (follow the "short test first" rule) |
| Storyboard doc → confirm → scene by scene | Already in video-explainer / video-talk | Add two columns to the storyboard table: "what this moment does" and "the object carried into the next shot" (everestchris6's storyboard requirement) |
| Independent critic review | Currently self-review | After rendering, dispatch a **sub-agent that has not seen the code** to read the contact sheet and output timestamped P0/P1/P2 issues, ending with ship or one more round |

### 5.2 Proposed new skills (5)

**Skill 1: `video-floorplan` (floor plan → CAD → 3D → sunlight, Three.js vertical)**
Input: a floor-plan image (picture or PDF) or a few sentences describing the layout. Step one: Claude reads the drawing and writes `plan.json` (wall segments, thickness, door/window positions and widths, room names and areas, orientation, floor height); **when a labelled dimension doesn't match the measured one, list the mismatches and ask the user to confirm instead of guessing** (borrowed from aayush4soni). The animation has four fixed acts (borrowed from cryptowluha, MrKindey and heyiamnick): (1) a pencil sketch drawn stroke by stroke on paper (sine wobble + double stroke); (2) conversion to a CAD blueprint (white lines, hidden edges dashed, dimension lines appearing one by one, area numbers rolling up); (3) walls extruded from the floor into white massing within their `[t0,t1]` windows, door and window openings cut, furniture dropped in room by room, camera kept at a 35–55° downward angle, the model on a base; (4) sunlight: sun azimuth and elevation computed from real latitude and date (winter/summer solstice) as a function of t, sweeping through a day with shadows moving across the floor, and a label for "living-room sunlight hours at the winter solstice". Everything follows the `draw(t)` pure-function convention, with labels on a 2D overlay. Around 9 lines of edge-tts narration, ending with "for illustration only, not a construction drawing". The repo already has `works/kp03_two-bedroom-floorplan/`, which can be used as the starting point for the template.

**Skill 2: `video-exploded` (3D exploded-view explainers for science/machines)**
Swappable subject: heart, engine, watch, phone, air conditioner, toilet cistern, the layers inside a wall… The prompt keeps aichrislee's three-part structure (exterior materials → name the "invisible internal parts" one by one → motion rules), but the interaction becomes a fixed timeline: orbit the exterior (3 s) → section plane cuts it open (3 s) → internal motion demo (heartbeat, pistons, as periodic functions) → layered explode with dashed leader-line labels, **each part paired with one counter-intuitive fact** (borrowed from 0xSpikez) → reassemble. Lighting is product-photography key light + rim light, glows and particles banned. Outputs include `parts.json` (part name, position, explode direction, one-line description, fact source); the script is generated from this file so captions and labels always agree.

**Skill 3: `video-zoom` (infinite zoom / scale comparison in one continuous shot)**
For continuous zooms like "from the desk to an atom", "Earth, Jupiter and the Sun side by side", "from a grain of rice to a granary" or "city → neighborhood → floor plan → wall layers". The core is a log-scale camera: `scale(t) = 10^(a + b·ease(t))`; each level is a scene that fades in and out as its scale is reached. A **scale ruler is always visible** on the side (borrowed from Acoramaa), and numbers are real data with sources cited. Either a 2D Canvas or a Three.js implementation works; levels connect by "the foreground object becomes the transition", with no cuts. Suits 20–45 second vertical videos with high completion rates.

**Skill 4: `video-qc` (render QC + independent critic)**
A QC tool shared by all code-animation skills, extending `render.py`: (1) determinism check (pick 5 random frames, render each twice, compare hashes); (2) contact sheet (16 frames across the whole video + dense sampling ±0.5 s around each transition); (3) freeze detection (runs of adjacent frames whose difference is below a threshold; alert over 0.5 s, and total frozen time per 30 seconds); (4) text checks (contrast ≥ 4.5:1, no overlapping text, key text not outside the safe zone); (5) audio (LUFS loudness, true peak, clipping, SFX never louder than music); (6) whether the first frame is a complete composition. After the script runs, dispatch a sub-agent that has not seen the code to review the contact sheet and output timestamped P0/P1/P2 issues and a "ship / one more round" verdict, and write a `qc_ledger.md` in the work's folder recording every round.

**Skill 5: `video-beat` (beat grid + code-synthesized sound design)**
For quote, beat-sync and product vertical videos. Analyze the BGM with numpy/librosa (preferably a royalty-free track around 120 BPM) to get the beat grid and the drop position, snap every cut to a beat, and start each move 0.05 s early so it lands exactly on the beat (borrowed from heyiamnick); SFX (pop, whoosh, landing thud, bell) can be synthesized in Python or taken from CC0 assets, aligned to events by peak; music ducks when narration plays; final -14 LUFS. Optional sub-frame motion blur (3 sub-frames + tmix). It can be combined with NFT_Chen's "beat-synced typography: one word per beat, orange text cutting in on black… the final hit" template, becoming a "pure-code version" of the existing video-quote line.

(Optional sixth) **`video-style-library` (a library of 10-second style clips)**: organize NFT_Chen's 15 Chinese-language templates, plus Lemo-Opuscar's style library (<https://github.com/lemomo-ai/lemo-opuscar>, which athemeroy describes as "43 styles"), into our own style library, each style with a reference `draw(t)` implementation and a sample frame, so each shot of a kp video can pick a style from the library.
